newsitem.title: USA: Fed Beige Book affirms outlook for steady US rates.
newsitem.headline: Fed Beige Book affirms outlook for steady US rates.

text.p: The Federal Reserve's Beige Book report on recent U.S. economic conditions confirmed the market forecast for steady U.S. interest rates in the near term, analysts said on Wednesday.
"It's again a story of strong growth trend, flat price trend, tight labor market trend and generally subdued wage pressures," said chief economist Lou Crandall at R.H. Wrightson and Associates.
Crandall was commenting on the Fed's report of economic conditions in the 50 U.S. states in June and July.
The Fed Board issues the report, compiled by the 12 Fed district banks, for discussion by the members of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) who next meet to set monetary policy on August 19.

All 33 economists polled this week by Reuters predicted the Fed will keep the federal funds rate unchanged at 5.50 percent -- its level since a 25-basis-point hike in March. A move on the 5.0-percent discount rate is not expected either.
The analysts cited the absence of inflationary pressures as the main reason for the steady rate forecast to which the rising dollar contributed somewhat.
"It's the same contrast that has fueled Treasury market moves back and forth for a couple years now," Crandall said.

The Wrightson economist pointed out the Treasury market has rallied and sold off since 1995 as strong economic data -- mainly the slide in the jobless rate -- raised fears of higher interest rates while surprising low inflation readings removed such concern.

"This Beige Book recapitulates the July employment report very well, with a combination of unsustainable job growth and wage increases below expectations," Crandall added. "It's not what we expected to see, but that's what we are getting.
Economists have explained the absence of wage-driven inflation despite record demand for labor by the return of scores of retired or discouraged workers to the workforce.
"This Beige Book does not alter the outlook for steady Fed policy in August," Crandall admitted. "The anomaly persists."
However, Crandall, echoing Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's caution, warned the low inflation story may just reflect transitory factors.
"We are not going to be able to entice 3/4 million ex-workers back into the labor force every year," predicted Crandall, who foresaw somewhat tighter credit before yearend.

Ethan Harris, senior economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc, agreed the Fed has no need to rush and hike rates in August -- an outlook that the Beige Boook did not alter. Harris, however, said the report was a little less market-supportive than expected.
"This Beige Book was a little bit less friendly than what we saw in May/early June mainly because growth was more brisk and consumer spending picked up," Harris said.
"These observations were expected. But the fact the Fed mentioned this right at the opening made it a little bit of a negative report," added Harris.
Harris predicted the Fed will tighten credit if growth accelerates above 3.0 percent, or if inflation perks ups.

"The Beige Book has more weight in the market than it has in actual policy thinking," said Harris, a former senior New York Fed staffer, who noted the report is almost never crucial for policy-making because it condenses the views from 12 district banks and tends to minimize the differences.

Harris said the prior Beige Book, prepared for the July meeting when the Fed kept rates unchanged, gave a surprisingly subdued reading on the still robust economy, while this one was closed to real conditions.
FOMC members also have access to two other books, the Green and the Blue one, that compile data and model-generated forecasts for policy-making purposes.
